Purely Torsional Nystagmus in a Patient 
with the Stiff-Man Syndrome: A Case Report 
Michael Quentin Stearns, Bethesda, MD; Stuart E. Sinoff, 
Washington, DC; Michael L. Rosenberg, Bethesda, MD 
Objectiue. Report of a case of stiff-man syndrome with purely 
torsional nystagmus, implying involvement of GABAergic cen- 
tral vestibular pathways. 
Background. The pathophysiology of stiff-man syndrome is 
thought to be related to an abnormality of the GABAergic inhibi- 
tion of alpha spinal motor neurons. There is experimental and 
clinical evidence that GABAergic neurons are also involved in 
central vestibular function. 
Case report. A 36-year-old male with a 2-year history of typi- 
cal stiff-man syndrome developed blurred vision. General neuro- 
logic examination showed changes of stiff-man syndrome, but 
was otherwise normal. Neuro-ophthalmologic examination 
demonstrated only a prominent pure counterclockwise torsional 
nystagmus. An enhanced MRI of the posterior fossa was normal. 
Conclusions. 1. Dysfunction of central vestibular pathways 
employing GABA as an inhibitory neurotransmitter may serve 
as a model for pure torsional nystagmus. 2. Stiff-man syndrome 
may involve GABAergic control of vestibular function as well as 
spinal alpha motor neurons.
